newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Remote Siberia region sees strong Buddhist revival.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Remote Siberia region sees strong Buddhist revival.

text.p: Dmitry knew exactly what he wanted to do after quitting the army, although his decision dismayed his parents and surprised his former comrades.

"My aim is to become a Buddhist monk. I have been reading up on Buddhism for many years and have visited several Buddhist countries," said Dmitry, a tall, sinewy 33-year-old with pensive blue eyes and close-cropped hair.

He is one of eight young Russians following a five-year course of study in Tibetan Buddhism at the Ivolginsk Datsan (monastery) in the rolling hills of Russia's autonomous republic of Buryatia in southern Siberia.
"Of course it was never easy sticking to Buddhist teachings in the environment of a Russian army barracks but nobody tried to stop me believing what I wanted," said Dmitry.
"My parents were not too pleased about me becoming a Buddhist. They think that if you are born a Christian that is the way you should stay," he added, grinning broadly.
Dmitry, who is from the Russian Far East, shares a sparsely furnished chalet in the monastery grounds with two other Russian students who have recently finished their military service.
REMOTE SIBERIAN REGION SEES BIG REVIVAL IN BUDDHISM

"It's much easier studying Buddhism here. It is the most important centre in Russia and we have a very good teacher, a Tibetan monk," said Alexei, who was having his hair shorn by their third room-mate, Vladislav.
The Dalai Lama, Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, who has visited the monastery, is the spiritual head of the Yellow Hat sect to which most Russian Buddhists belong.

"We have seen an upsurge of interest in Buddhism over the past 10 years since the opening up of the old Soviet Union. Some 16 new temples have been built," said Bato Tsidipov, an expert on religion who works for Buryatia's regional government.
"People come from all parts of Russia, Ukraine and beyond to visit the monasteries and temples and to study Buddhism."
It is not surprising that Buryatia, lying between Siberia's vast Lake Baikal and the Mongolian border, should be at the forefront of Buddhism's revival in the former Soviet Union.

Its indigenous people, closely related to the Mongols, began converting to Tibetan Tantric Buddhism in the 17th century and the region boasted more than 100 temples and dozens of monasteries before the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.
COMMUNISTS PERSECUTED BUDDHISTS, THEN RELENTED
During his brutal clampdown on religion in the 1930s, Soviet dictator Josef Stalin sent thousands of lamas (priests) to the Gulag and destroyed scores of monasteries and temples.

But, in an unusually tolerant gesture, and in recognition of the Buryat people's contribution in World War Two, Stalin allowed a couple of Buddhist monasteries, including Ivolginsk, to be rebuilt in 1946.
In the later Soviet period official policy towards Buddhists relaxed and monks were allowed to travel to Mongolia to study.
"The communists saw Buddhism as less threatening than some other religions because of its flexibility and scientific approach," said Tsidipov.
Now monks travel further afield, to India, Japan and other countries, to study and deepen their contact with different Buddhist traditions.

Lama Yeshe-Nima Namzhilov, who helps run a Buddhist centre in the regional capital Ulan-Ude, said some 500 people from across the former Soviet Union recently gathered near Lake Baikal for a seminar given by an eminent Tibetan monk.
"It was quite a shock for some Buryats to see Buddhists from outside their region. They realised that their faith is far more widespread than they had thought," he chuckled.
BURYATIA HAS LONG TRADITION OF RELIGIOUS TOLERANCE

The Buryats, whose brand of Buddhism is interwoven with animistic Shamanist beliefs, make up only a quarter of their republic's population -- Russians are the biggest ethnic group -- but they are not the only ones visiting the Buddhist temples.
"Many local Russians go to Ivolginsk and other Buddhist shrines to pray and seek blessings, just as the Buryats go to (Russian) Orthodox churches," said Tsidipov.

Buryatia's tradition of religious harmony -- Christians, Buddhists, Shamanists worshipping quietly alongside each other -- has helped make it an oasis of political stability in contrast to some of Russia's other ethnically-based autonomous regions, notably Chechnya, Tsidipov added.
BUDDHIST ART TROVE WITNESS TO RICH RELIGIOUS PAST
Ulan Ude, in most respects a typically drab Soviet-style city, is home to Russia's richest collection of Buddhist art.

Housed in a former Russian Orthodox cathedral, the artefacts -- which include Tantric sculptures, thankas (icon tapestries), masks, vestments and sacred texts -- were mostly culled from Buddhist temples and monasteries shut down by the Bolsheviks.
The collection also contains Shamanist artefacts, including the bells and sacred staff used by the Shaman -- an intercessor between the human and spiritual worlds -- during his trances.
"This collection represents just a small part of what did exist. So much was destroyed," said curator Lyuba Levitina. "But now in Buryatia we are trying to return to our spiritual roots."
For Dmitry and his friends, their soldiering days behind them, Buryatia's rich religious heritage has a broader, more universal appeal.
"Many more Russians would come here to study Buddhism but they don't know about it. They lack information. But when I finish here I will go back and spread the word," said Dmitry.
"The religion you choose, if any, ultimately depends on who you are, your character and inclinations. I studied many religions but felt somehow nearer to Buddhism.
"The most important thing is peace and having the chance and the freedom to develop yourself in the way you want."
